title: The Interior of Milton Flats
premise: Yara Reyes has tuned the pianos of Milton Flats for five years, learning its residents' secrets through pipes and floorboards while saying almost nothing about what he knows. When Mr. Okonkwo-Bass, the last fluent speaker of a dying language, asks Yara to become his final student before the building's demolition, Yara must choose between the invisibility that has kept him safe and the loyalty that demands he bear witness. As demolition day approaches, a developer's cover-up of toxic conditions forces Yara to break his silence publicly. The novel ends with Yara recording Mr. O's last words in the empty lobby, then speaking them aloud at the city hearing—saying goodbye properly, out loud, as the flats come down and his found family scatters but holds.
about_author: Marguerite Nystrom is a former building superintendent who spent eleven years listening to the mechanical heartbeats of pre-war apartment houses. She writes from a converted boiler room in upstate New York.

chapters.title: The Pitch Pipe
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. He tunes the lobby piano and reads the building's mood through its radiators—each unit has a voice. Establishes his ritual of near-silence: he knows Mrs. Adeyemi's eviction notice is coming before she does. Emotional beat: comfort found in being unheard.

chapters.title: Unit 4B Speaks in Tongues
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Sent to tune a piano no one plays, he finds Mr. Okonkwo-Bass singing to himself in a language Yara can't place. The old man catches him listening—and instead of anger, asks him to sit. Beat: first crack in Yara's invisibility.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, with flashbacks to the brother he failed to defend years ago. He practices phrases to Mr. O and abandons each one. Meanwhile tenants whisper about a new owner, Corliss Development. Beat: the cost of silence made personal.

chapters.title: The Student Question
chapters.summary: Mr. O's POV. He formally asks Yara to become his last student; his daughter in Lagos stopped answering, and the language dies with him otherwise. Yara deflects. Beat: hope offered and flinched from.

chapters.title: Radiator Hymns
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. First lessons: not vocabulary but listening. Mr. O teaches through the building itself—pipes as grammar, knocks as proverbs. Yara begins repeating words under his breath at night. Beat: reluctant joy.

chapters.title: The Demolition Date
chapters.summary: Mrs. Adeyemi's POV. Notices appear: Milton Flats closes in six months. Tenants organize loosely; Yara attends a meeting but says nothing useful. Beat: guilt sharpening into something actionable.

chapters.title: What the Pipes Knew First
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Tuning upper floors, he smells the mold behind fresh paint and hears coughing through shared walls—Corliss is hiding habitability violations. He knows; he almost says it to a tenant; he doesn't. Beat: silence becomes complicity.

chapters.title: Mr. O's Box
chapters.summary: Mr. O's POV. He shows Yara a shoebox of cassette tapes—forty years of recorded stories, songs, arguments. He wants them transcribed before the end. Yara agrees, his first real yes. Beat: inheritance accepted.

chapters.title: The Tenant Ledger
chapters.summary: Dual focus via Yara's POV. He starts a secret notebook documenting violations, unit by unit—a tuner's log doubling as evidence. Teenager Dez catches him writing and assumes he's a spy for Corliss. Beat: loyalty misread as betrayal.

chapters.title: Dez
chapters.summary: Dez's POV. The kid who runs errands for everyone confronts Yara in the stairwell. A grudging alliance forms when Yara shows him the notebook. Beat: found family expanding against Yara's will.

chapters.title: The Language of Leaving
chapters.summary: Mr. O's POV. Lessons deepen; Mr. O reveals why his daughter left—the language carries a family shame he won't explain yet. His health falters mid-lesson. Beat: mortality entering the room.

chapters.title: Inspection
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. A city inspector tours the building; tenants are coached to stay quiet. Yara stands in a doorway holding his notebook and says nothing as the inspector passes. That night he can't sleep. Beat: the almost-saying reaches its limit.

chapters.title: Cassette Nine
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Transcribing tape nine, Yara hears Mr. O describe—in the dying language—the brother Yara lost, a story Mr. O somehow knows. The old man has been teaching him forgiveness all along. Beat: devastating tenderness.

chapters.title: The Daughter Calls
chapters.summary: Mr. O's POV. His daughter phones during a lesson; Mr. O lets it ring out, then finally tells Yara the shame: he renounced the language publicly decades ago to survive, and taught her none of it. Beat: truth as inheritance, however painful.

chapters.title: Corliss Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: Mrs. Adeyemi's POV. Buyout offers arrive with deadlines and veiled threats; some neighbors sign. Dez's family wavers. Yara's ledger could change the math—but using it means exposure. Beat: the community fracturing under pressure.

chapters.title: What Yara Almost Said
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. At a tenant meeting, someone accuses him of hoarding information. He nearly reads from the ledger, then folds it away again. Mr. O watches from the back and later says only: 'A word kept past its season rots.' Beat: the rebuke that breaks him open.

chapters.title: The Leak
chapters.summary: Dez's POV. Dez photographs pages of Yara's ledger and sends them to a local journalist without asking. The story runs: hidden toxicity, falsified inspections. Chaos and vindication hit the building at once. Beat: truth escaping its keeper.

chapters.title: Hearing Notice
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. The city schedules an emergency hearing; tenants are asked to testify. Corliss lawyers circle. Yara is asked to speak about what he heard through the walls—he is the witness they need. Beat: terror and readiness arriving together.

chapters.title: The Last Lesson
chapters.summary: Mr. O's POV. Hospitalized, Mr. O gives his final lesson from a cot: how to say goodbye in the language—there is a specific phrase, used only for permanent partings. He makes Yara repeat it until it's true. Beat: preparation for both goodbyes at once.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Climax. At the hearing, Yara testifies—not reading the ledger but telling the building's history as Mr. O taught him to hear it, opening with the goodbye phrase spoken aloud. The room goes silent, then the tenants rise. Beat: the almost-said finally said.

chapters.title: Demolition Day
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs braided. The flats come down; tenants gather with coffee and folding chairs. Mr. O, discharged for the day, stands beside Yara. They speak the farewell phrase together as the wall falls. Beat: grief and gratitude inseparable.

chapters.title: The Second Speaker
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, epilogue. Months later, Yara records himself speaking the language for Mr. O's daughter, who has begun calling. In his new apartment, the radiators have a different voice, and he answers it. Beat: silence transformed into transmission.
